scenario: The infra track has 10 papers today, 6 with deep dives. The common thread is keeping LLM and retrieval services stable, cheap and trustworthy under tight resources. ZipFusion lets attention read a losslessly compressed KV cache directly, and BellowsKV lets several layers share one compressed input. Microsoft's HiLO moves degradation from the service level to the product level. PayPal's Cosmos gateway puts access, budgets and policy for many model vendors in one place. CoLoc decides where vector data should live, and TrustANN checks whether retrieved results can be trusted. Inference serving teams can start with ZipFusion and BellowsKV, and platform governance teams with Cosmos.

papers.title: HiLO: Towards Product-Level Graceful Degradation with a Quality-Aware, Load-Aware Control Framework
papers.authors: Knut Magne Risvik, Zhuowei Li, Nirupam Purushothama, Hunter Su, Greg Dunham, Yan Reznikov
papers.abstract: Graceful degradation is a key mechanism employed by large-scale systems to handle overload conditions. Its importance has grown further as GPU-intensive LLM inference introduces persistent capacity constraints that cannot be addressed through provisioning alone. Common degradation approaches rely on service-level mechanisms such as load shedding and circuit breakers, or on feature-level switches (some manually controlled) to preserve availability and quality. While effective at protecting services, such approaches lead to untestable product states and thereby unpredictable product quality. We present HiLO (High Load Optimizer), an automated product-level degradation system designed to handle graceful degradation at scale. HiLO maps observed load to a product state lattice: a small set of pre-validated product states, partially ordered by degradation severity. Dependencies are resolved at design time enabling deterministic and continuous control without requiring runtime dependency discovery. The same abstraction applies unchanged across heterogeneous services, including GPU-intensive deep models, LLMs and their serving layers. At Microsoft, HiLO is deployed in Bing (serving over a billion monthly active users), where it manages on average two traffic surges per week across all datacenters, bounding OneDCG (relevance) drop to under 0.5 points (the operational target) even under sustained load exceeding 2$\times$ baseline peak. HiLO complements existing service-level protections with product-level coordination and makes product quality measurable, testable and predictable.
papers.summary: During traffic spikes, each service degrades on its own, so every service survives while the product's quality can collapse. Microsoft's HiLO moves degradation from the service level to the product level. It predefines a few validated product states. Each state sets a level for every service, such as dropping some features, reducing fan-out or using a cheaper model. At runtime services report load and a central controller picks one state. ==The unit of degradation should be the product, not the service==. It went through 9 real traffic surges. The largest hit 2.38 times baseline peak, and Bing's relevance metric OneDCG, a normalized ranking-quality score, dropped at most 0.425 points, inside the 0.5-point operating limit.

deep_reading.title: HiLO: Towards Product-Level Graceful Degradation with a Quality-Aware, Load-Aware Control Framework

papers.title: Cross-Modal Data Co-Locality for Heterogeneous Storage Systems
papers.abstract: Distributed vector stores increasingly serve multimodal workloads whose representations are jointly accessed but independently partitioned and placed. As a result, cross-modal physical locality remains largely unoptimized. Multimodal queries can incur remote accesses and cross-tier data movement even when each modality's ANN search remains efficient. We present Coloc, a storage-management layer that makes cross-modal access locality a first-class data-layout signal. A Cross-Modal Access Graph combines semantic affinity, co-access, and temporal behavior. A movement-aware optimizer places frequently co-accessed vectors under capacity and topology constraints. A migration manager adapts placement as workloads shift by weighing locality gains against migration cost. A confidence-gated prefetcher hides remaining slow-tier latency. Coloc operates above existing ANN indexes without modifying embeddings, search, or retrieval semantics. We deploy Coloc on a multi-tier AWS testbed spanning GPU, NUMA-DRAM, NVMe, and S3. Coloc substantially reduces data movement and query latency while leaving ANN retrieval unchanged. Under a scheduled workload shift, its migration manager matches the locality of periodic global reorganization while moving 5.9x less data and completing 3.9x faster.
papers.summary: A multimodal query first searches text vectors and then fetches the matching image vectors. Both nearest-neighbor searches are fast. The slow part is moving data when the two vectors sit in different storage tiers. CoLoc changes neither the vectors nor the index. It only decides which tier holds what, keeping vectors that are queried together in the same tier. ==It optimizes where data lives, not where to search==. On a four-tier setup, cross-tier queries fell from 73.04% to 0, and end-to-end latency fell 24.8% at a half-multimodal mix, with recall unchanged.

deep_reading.title: Cross-Modal Data Co-Locality for Heterogeneous Storage Systems

papers.title: Failure-Resilient and Verifiable Distributed Approximate Nearest-Neighbor Retrieval
papers.abstract: Distributed vector databases increasingly support security-sensitive applications, yet existing systems primarily protect index integrity or replica availability rather than the trustworthiness of retrieved results. Consequently, a compromised replica can return a plausible but manipulated result that remains cryptographically valid, while conventional replication and Byzantine defenses do not directly establish whether the retrieved results are trustworthy. We present TrustANN, a middleware layer that provides query-level trust for distributed approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) retrieval without modifying the underlying ANN algorithm. TrustANN introduces three complementary protocols: TrustBind, which verifies retrieval trust from authenticated, consistent, and failure-domain-independent replica evidence; CoordShift, which asynchronously constructs reusable coordination epochs outside the query critical path; and AvailGuard, which performs bounded recovery when replicas are unavailable, stale, or conflicting while preserving the trust criterion. Queries are marked Trusted only when sufficient independent evidence exists for every relevant shard; otherwise, TrustANN returns Unverified. On an AWS deployment using distributed FAISS HNSW, TrustANN reduces retrieval attack success rate from 1.000 to 0.000 under the tested Byzantine-retrieval attack with two-of-three replica verification. The verification layer increases clean p95 latency by only 9.36%. Under replica crashes, TrustANN maintains trusted retrieval through 33% failures and correctly returns Unverified when sufficient evidence is unavailable.
papers.summary: Replicas in a distributed vector database keep results available but do not make them trustworthy. A compromised replica can return validly signed but tampered nearest neighbors. TrustANN adds middleware above the router. For each shard it greedily picks a set of replica replies that meets a set minimum size, scores high on pairwise similarity (candidate overlap plus rank agreement), and spans a set number of failure domains such as availability zones. If it falls short, it asks fresh independent replicas, and otherwise returns an explicit unverified status. ==Replicas being online does not make results trustworthy==. In a multi-node test, tampered results accepted as trusted fell from 100% to 0, while p95 latency rose only 9.36% under normal load.

deep_reading.title: Failure-Resilient and Verifiable Distributed Approximate Nearest-Neighbor Retrieval

papers.title: BellowsKV: One Latent for Many Layers, Expanded on Demand
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) now serve as the backbone of agents that reason over many turns, call tools, and pursue long-horizon tasks. To avoid recomputation, a model stores the attention keys and values of all past tokens in a key-value (KV) cache. Each layer maintains its own cache, so KV-cache memory can become the main bottleneck for GPU serving. Most compression methods operate within a single layer, by quantizing the cache entries, reducing the channel dimension, or evicting less important tokens. All three lose substantial accuracy at high compression ratios. Cross-layer methods share one compressed cache across adjacent layers to go beyond this limit. However, these methods also degrade sharply at high compression ratios. We find that the KV-cache representations of adjacent layers are quite different, whereas the input hidden states of adjacent layers are highly similar. We also find that, under the same memory budget, reducing the dimension of this shared latent loses far more accuracy than quantizing it. Based on these findings, we propose BellowsKV, a training-free method that maps the hidden states of n adjacent layers to one shared latent per token. At inference time, each layer reads its own keys and values from this latent through a layer-specific projection. We keep the latent at full dimension and compress it in two other ways: BellowsKV-Quant stores the latent at low precision, which is nearly lossless because the latent has no dominant outlier channels; BellowsKV-Evict makes one shared eviction decision per block, because the layers rank token importance very similarly. Across Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B and Qwen2.5-7B, BellowsKV-Quant retains about 99% of full-cache accuracy at 3.6x compression and 97-98% at 13-14x, where the strongest cross-layer method retains at most 84% at 16x. Code: https://github.com/MorrisZJ/BellowsKV
papers.summary: In long-context inference, the largest memory cost is often the per-layer KV cache, the keys and values attention stores for every past token. BellowsKV observes that caches of adjacent layers differ, but the hidden states that produce them are similar. So it shares the input, not the cache. For each token, it concatenates the hidden states of n adjacent layers and multiplies them by a compression matrix, giving one shared vector that replaces those layers' caches. Each layer has its own restore matrix that maps the shared vector back to its keys and values. Both are solved once offline from calibration data to minimize reconstruction error, with no training. ==Share the input, not the cache==. On 3 models it keeps over 97% of accuracy at about 14x compression, with decoding speed close to uncompressed.

deep_reading.title: BellowsKV: One Latent for Many Layers, Expanded on Demand

papers.title: ZipFusion: Fusing Lossless KV Decompression with Attention for Efficient LLM Decoding
papers.authors: Yuetao Chen, Peng Wang, Hong Xu
papers.abstract: The key-value (KV) cache places growing demands on GPU memory capacity and bandwidth as large language models serve longer contexts and more concurrent requests. Its footprint limits concurrency, while repeated KV reads during attention can make decoding memory-bandwidth bound. Prior lossless KV cache compression methods reduce transfers between devices but restore the uncompressed KV cache in GPU memory before attention. They therefore leave these repeated KV reads unchanged and require additional work and memory for decompression. We present ZipFusion, which enables attention to consume the losslessly compressed KV cache directly. ZipFusion co-designs the compression format and attention kernel to reduce the bytes read from GPU memory during attention. The kernel reconstructs the original values directly in registers using simple bit operations, avoiding a separate decompression pass and easing the memory-bandwidth bound. ZipFusion also reassigns memory freed by compression across layers to store additional KV cache. Its memory manager reserves space for ongoing generation and makes the remaining capacity available to new requests. We implement ZipFusion on top of FlashInfer and integrate it with SGLang. On an NVIDIA H100, ZipFusion achieves about 1.25x speedup over FlashInfer in decode attention. With 8K context, it improves model decode throughput by up to 26.3% over uncompressed SGLang under the same GPU memory budget. At each method's largest supported batch, it also delivers up to 2.76x the throughput of the best-performing lossless KV cache compression baseline.
papers.summary: Most of the gain from lossless KV cache compression is eaten by decompression. Earlier methods restore the full cache on the GPU, so attention still reads uncompressed data. In ZipFusion, attention reads compressed data directly The format compresses only the exponent bits of 16-bit floats, which cluster in a narrow range, and keeps the fraction bits as is. Attention rebuilds the exponents in registers with a few integer adds and shifts, giving bit-identical values. ==Lossless compression can make decoding faster, not just cheaper to move==. On an H100 the kernel is about 1.25x faster than FlashInfer, and at 8K context decode throughput beats uncompressed SGLang by 26.3%, bit for bit identical.

deep_reading.title: ZipFusion: Fusing Lossless KV Decompression with Attention for Efficient LLM Decoding

papers.title: Governing Enterprise AI Traffic at Scale: Design and Operation of a Policy-Driven, Multi-Vendor LLM Gateway on Envoy
papers.authors: Mithun Sasidharan, Srinivasan Manoharan, Rupesh Thakur, Abhinav TK, Ashwin Hegde, Anand Gautam
papers.abstract: Large organizations consume large language models (LLMs) from several vendors at once, each with its own API dialect, credential model, streaming protocol and pricing. Integrated directly, this heterogeneity yields credential sprawl, format lock-in, unbounded spend and inconsistent governance. We present the design and production operation of the Cosmos LLM Gateway, the governed entry point for enterprise LLM traffic at PayPal. Built on Envoy, it splits work by latency profile: I/O-bound control decisions (authentication, credential brokering, policy and budget evaluation) run in an out-of-process external-processing service, while wire-format translation, token metering and prompt-cache shaping run in-proxy as a Rust WebAssembly filter, so that, by default, streamed response body chunks never wait on an out-of-process call. Models, providers and prices are largely validated data rather than code. Governance is declarative policy evaluated by Open Policy Agent and managed through a control plane with role-scoped authoring, approvals, pilots, shadow-mode rollout, usage notifications and versioned policy bundles. For use cases that require it, a data-loss-prevention layer can block, redact or pseudonymize detected sensitive content before it reaches a provider. Spend scopes are views over per-model usage counters, so a new budget applies to spend already recorded in its window without migration. As of September 2026, the gateway serves more than 12,000 developers and hundreds of business use cases, handling roughly 200 billion tokens per day across more than 100 models at 99.999% availability to business. In a benchmark of the core request path against a synthetic upstream, it adds a median of 4 ms and a p99 of 11 ms of overhead at more than 2,200 requests per second on two 4-vCPU instances. We report the architecture, policy model, evaluation and lessons learned.
papers.summary: When a company uses models from several vendors and every app integrates them directly, keys spread, switching models needs code changes, and spend goes unmanaged. PayPal's Cosmos gateway is built on the Envoy proxy. Slow decisions such as auth, budgets and policy run outside the proxy. Format translation and token counting run inside it, so no streamed chunk waits on an external call. ==The hard part of a gateway is governance, not routing==. It serves over 12,000 developers and about 200 billion tokens a day, adding only 4 ms of median latency in load tests.

deep_reading.title: Governing Enterprise AI Traffic at Scale: Design and Operation of a Policy-Driven, Multi-Vendor LLM Gateway on Envoy

papers.title: Prefetch-Steered Routing: Deterministic Cache-Aware Expert Selection for Offloaded Mixture-of-Experts Decoding
papers.abstract: When a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model does not fit in GPU memory, batch-1 decoding is dominated by copying expert weights from host memory. Cache-aware routing reduces these copies by biasing the router toward resident experts, but combined with asynchronous prefetching it makes the model's outputs depend on transfer timing, so a harness that does not simulate that timing no longer evaluates the deployed model. We propose prefetch-steered routing (PSR): routing conditions on a deterministic logical cache, into which at most n experts predicted by the next layer's router are inserted per layer and token; physical copies affect only latency. On OLMoE-1B-7B with 50% and 25% of experts resident on an RTX 4090, PSR decodes 2.2-2.3x faster than exact routing with LRU and 25-30% faster than the Cache-Prior operating point, with mean benchmark differences of +0.1 and +0.5 points (95% lower bounds -0.8 and -0.3). In greedy generation its lead over Cache-Prior depends on the workload and reverses on HumanEval at 50% residency. On Moonlight-16B-A3B, PSR is 1.9x faster than exact routing with LRU at 37.5% residency and, at the latency of Cache-Prior, significantly better on three of eight benchmarks. On Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, where copies are cheap relative to computation, PSR keeps its advantage over Cache-Prior on the likelihood benchmarks but not its speed. Distillation-trained gates did not help. Speculative decoding with block-level expert selection was slower than PSR with a 1B autoregressive drafter on OLMoE, but with a block drafter on Qwen3.6 it was 2.1-2.9x faster than any autoregressive configuration with at most its GPU memory on the 64 prompts we timed.
papers.summary: When a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model does not fit in GPU memory, single-request decoding is dominated by copying expert weights from host memory. Routing biased toward resident experts cuts copies. Combined with asynchronous prefetching, though, outputs depend on transfer timing, so offline evaluation no longer matches the deployed model. PSR routes on a deterministic logical cache. At each layer, the current hidden state is fed to the next layer's router to predict its experts, and 1 or 2 of them enter the logical cache. Each layer's logical cache holds as many experts as there are GPU slots, and when full it evicts the expert with the lowest moving average of past router choices. In the next layer, cached experts get a fixed bonus added to their router scores. The cache depends only on token history, not on when copies finish. Physical copies follow it as prefetches and affect only speed. ==Make outputs deterministic first, then speed up with the cache==. On an RTX 4090 with OLMoE, it decodes over 2.2x faster than exact routing with LRU eviction, with benchmark scores essentially unchanged.

papers.title: A new paradigm for inference acceleration: inside Volcano Engine EIC, a high-performance distributed KV cache
papers.abstract: Elastic Instant Cache (EIC) is a high-performance distributed KV cache service built by Volcano Engine's storage team for large language model inference.
papers.summary: Many inference instances recomputing the same long prefix is a common waste in serving clusters. Volcano Engine's EIC (Elastic Instant Cache) is a distributed KV cache service for LLM inference. Its role is to keep the key-value cache computed during inference in a separate distributed cache layer. Multiple inference instances can then share and reuse it instead of recomputing long prefixes. ==Moving the KV cache out of single-GPU memory into a shared storage service== has become a clear direction for inference infrastructure. Teams running multi-instance serving, long context or multi-turn chat can use it as a product reference.

papers.title: 3 Ways to Boost MoE Inference on NVIDIA DGX Spark
papers.abstract: Generating tokens faster starts with identifying what limits inference performance. In the batch-size-1 evaluation of Ling-3.0-flash from Inclusion AI on NVIDIA...
papers.summary: When decoding one request at a time, the slow part is often reading weights, not compute. NVIDIA optimized the mixture-of-experts model Ling-3.0-flash on DGX Spark. Profiling showed weight reads were the bottleneck, mainly in expert computation and the output-layer projection. So all three techniques read fewer weights or produce more tokens per step. They swap in a faster expert kernel, quantize the output layer to 8 bits online, and use the model's built-in multi-token prediction for speculative decoding. ==Profile the bottleneck first, then cut weight reads where it hurts==. Combined, they raise decode throughput 42.5% on GSM8K and cut mean latency 24.5%, with no measurable accuracy change.

papers.title: How NVIDIA Minerva Turns Telemetry Chaos Into Peak GPU Yield
papers.abstract: AI Factories are some of the most technologically complex operational environments ever created. Hundreds of thousands of GPUs, NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet...
papers.summary: In large-scale training, one GPU running a little hot or one network port quietly degrading can slow an entire synchronous job. Such gray failures often trigger no fixed threshold. NVIDIA's Minerva merges telemetry from GPUs, network, storage and jobs into a live knowledge graph. Machine learning models flag devices that behave differently from their peers, The graph then shows which alerts share a dependency path, such as nodes behind one switch running one job, and merges them into one incident. ==Correlating alerts by topology finds root causes faster than checking thresholds one by one==. In one case, 81 alerts collapsed into 1 incident, saving an estimated 54 hours of cluster uptime.
